summary: Describes a scheme to packetize an H.263 video stream for transport using RTP. It also describes the SDP parameters for the H.263 video codec. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains how to cut H.263 video into little packets for internet delivery and put it back together.

questions: what is the rtp payload format for h.263
what is the p bit in the h.263 rtp header
difference between h263-1998 and h263-2000 media types
subtitle: How to carry H.263, H.263+ and H.263++ video in RTP packets, with built-in tricks for surviving packet loss.

tldr.problem: H.263 video streams must be split across RTP packets in a way that stays decodable when packets are lost, while supporting the many coding options added in the 1998 and 2000 versions.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP packet gets a 16-bit payload header whose P bit stands in for the two zero bytes of a start code, plus optional VRC information and an optional copy of the picture header for resynchronization.
tldr.outcome: New H.263 implementations SHALL use this format. It obsoletes RFC 2429, and RFC 2190 is moved to Historic status.

today: RFC 4629 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2007. It obsoletes RFC 2429, and its text says new H.263 implementations SHALL use this format instead of RFC 2190. The metadata for this site lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Scope and Relationship to Older Formats
sections.content:
This document specifies an RTP payload format for video based on the 1998 and 2000 versions of ITU-T Recommendation H.263. Because those versions are a superset of the 1996 syntax, the format can also carry 1996 H.263 and is recommended for that by new implementations.

It replaces the format in RFC 2190, which some existing implementations still use and which can help for backward compatibility. New implementations supporting H.263 SHALL use the format described here. RFC 2190 is moved to Historic status in RFC 4628. The document obsoletes RFC 2429 and updates the media type registrations in RFC 3555.
sections.plainLanguage: There was an older way to send this video. This RFC is the newer way, and anyone building something new should use it.

sections.title: New H.263 Features That Affect Packetization
sections.content:
The RFC calls the 1998 version of H.263 H.263+ and the 2000 version H.263++. The options with the most impact on packetization are the slice structured mode, independent segment decoding, reference picture selection and scalability.

Slices let the encoder fragment at macroblock boundaries and fit data to packet sizes. Independent segment decoding makes each segment decodable on its own, so errors do not spread. Reference picture selection lets a picture be predicted from an older reference, and RTCP feedback from RFC 4585 MAY be used as a back channel. Scalability comes in temporal, SNR and spatial forms. H.263++ added interlace mode and profiles and levels.
sections.plainLanguage: The newer versions of the video format added extra tricks to make pictures tougher against lost pieces. This RFC has to make room for all of them.

sections.title: Using RTP for H.263+
sections.content:
The encoder output is packetized directly, with one exception: when a packet's payload begins with a Picture, GOB, Slice, EOS or EOSBS start code, the first 2 all-zero bytes are removed and replaced by setting the P bit in the payload header. Each layer of a scalable stream may use its own IP address and port, with timing relations carried in the RTP timestamp.

The marker bit is 1 when the packet carries the end of the current frame. The timestamp uses a 90 kHz clock and is the same on successive packets of one frame. A picture clock frequency is expressed as 1800000/(cd*cf) pictures per second, where cd is an integer from 1 to 127 and cf is 1000 or 1001. The RFC gives time increments of 3003 for 30/1.001 Hz NTSC and 3600 for 25 Hz PAL.
sections.plainLanguage: Every picture starts with a fixed beginning that is always the same. Instead of sending it each time, the RFC just flips a switch that means it was there.

sections.title: The Payload Header
sections.content:
Each RTP packet carries exactly one H.263+ video packet, and the payload header is always present. The general header is 16 bits: RR (5 bits, reserved, SHALL be zero), P (1), V (1), PLEN (6) and PEBIT (3).

P marks a picture, GOB, slice or sequence-end start whose two leading zero bytes were omitted. V says an 8-bit Video Redundancy Coding (VRC) field follows. PLEN is the length in bytes of an extra picture header attached to the payload header, and PEBIT says how many bits to ignore in its last byte. The minimum header length is 16 bits.

The VRC field holds TID (3 bits, thread ID, up to 7 threads), Trun (4 bits, a packet counter per thread, modulo 16) and S (1 bit, marks a sync frame). Independent threads limit damage to the thread that lost a packet, and thread 0 is the canonical one.
sections.plainLanguage: Each parcel has a tiny label. It says whether the parcel starts a new piece, and it can hold a spare copy of the picture's cover page.

sections.title: Packet Types and Packetization Schemes
sections.content:
A picture segment packet (P=1) starts at a Picture, GOB or slice start code. A sequence ending packet starts at an EOS or EOSBS code and always has P=1 and PLEN=0. A follow-on packet (P=0) carries data that does not start at a synchronization point, so it is not independently decodable. If the preceding packet is lost, a receiver may discard the follow-on packet, though scanning its interior for resync codes is better.

An extra picture header (PLEN>0) is normally attached only when the picture header in the bitstream is incomplete (UFEP=000) and the attached copy is complete (UFEP=001), or on GOB and slice packets for resilience. Only the last six bits of the picture start code, 100000, are included, and the receiver prepends sixteen zero bits. Encoders are discouraged from sending EOS and EOSBS, since losing such a packet may be misread as losing essential video data.

If a whole coded frame fits in one packet, only picture segment packets are needed, which is often possible for QCIF with typical packet sizes around 1500 bytes. Otherwise, follow-on packets give minimal overhead when loss is low, while splitting into slices or GOBs gives resync points that survive loss.
sections.plainLanguage: Some parcels start a fresh piece of the picture, and some are just the middle of a piece. The middle ones are useless if the earlier part is lost.

sections.title: Media Types and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC registers video/H263-1998 and video/H263-2000. Optional parameters include picture sizes SQCIF, QCIF, CIF, CIF4 and CIF16 with an MPI (minimum picture interval) from 1 to 32, plus CUSTOM, PAR, CPCF, BPP, HRD and annex flags F, I, J, T, K, N and P. With no annex given, the stream is Baseline H.263.

H263-2000 adds PROFILE (0 through 10), LEVEL (0 through 100) and INTERLACE. A system specifying a PROFILE MUST specify the LEVEL, and PROFILE and LEVEL SHALL NOT be used with other optional parameters. A decoder that supports a profile SHALL also support profile 0.

In SDP the media name MUST be video, the encoding name H263-1998 or H263-2000, and the clock rate 90000. A receiver that gives no picture size SHOULD be ready to receive QCIF with MPI=1. Parameters offered first are most preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a video call starts, each side lists what picture sizes and tricks it can handle, with its favourite first.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The format is subject to the security considerations of RFC 3550 and the applicable profile such as RFC 3551. Confidentiality is achieved by encryption, which may be performed after compression because compression is applied end to end.

A potential denial-of-service threat exists for compression techniques with non-uniform receiver-end computational load: an attacker can inject pathological datagrams that are costly to decode. Authentication of at least the RTP packet is RECOMMENDED. A security review of this payload format found no additional considerations beyond those in the RTP specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could send tricky packets that are very hard to unpack, so it is wise to check who really sent each one.

fields.name: RR
fields.desc: Reserved; SHALL be zero and ignored by receivers.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: Start of a picture, segment or sequence end; two zero bytes omitted.

fields.name: PLEN
fields.desc: Length in bytes of the extra picture header.

fields.name: PEBIT
fields.desc: Bits to ignore in the last byte of the picture header.
